Rivoli hummingbirds (Eugenes fulgens) emerge from the embryonated egg after a documented incubation period of 17 days [ab = 17 days] when incubated at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], a value consistent with the altricial developmental mode typical of trochilids. This species, one of the largest hummingbirds in North America, begins life as a remarkably small nestling. Upon hatching, the newly emerged chick weighs approximately 0.85 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.85 grams], a modest initial mass that belies the rapid growth trajectory that will ensue. However, the mass of the freshly laid egg itself, representing the fertilised ovum before extensive albumen deposition, has been recorded at 0.984 grams [Ww0 = 0.984 grams], indicating a substantial investment in yolk reserves prior to the onset of incubation. These initial masses reflect the energetic capital provided by the female before the brooded nestling begins to receive parental provisioning.

The developmental milestones of the nestling chick underpin the species' life history, particularly when measured under conditions approximating an active adult's metabolic temperature. At a stable body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a predictable sequence of events unfolds. The altricial nestling reaches the point of first flight and gradually achieves nutritional independence after approximately 20 days from hatching [tx = approximately 20 days from hatching], marking the fledgling p at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]recursor stage. This relatively brief period in the nest is followed by a longer phase of somatic development. The growing juvenile bird, now a pre-reproductive juvenile, does not achieve sexual maturation until considerably later. Puberty, defined here as the onset of gonadal swelling and reproductive activation, occurs roughly 60 days after hatching [tp = roughly 60 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a delay that reflects the substantial energetic investment required to complete the growth of flight muscles and the complex aerodynamic apparatus.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is pronounced in this species, and the ultimate wet weight, or asymptotic adult body mass, differs markedly between the sexes. Adult females, which are the smaller sex, attain a maximum recorded body mass of 5.2 grams [Wwi = 5.2 grams]. In contrast, adult males, which are known for their aggressive territorial displays and larger overall frame, reach a significantly greater asymptotic mass of 7.9 grams [Wwi = 7.9 grams]. This difference of more than 50% in adult mass is among the most extreme examples of reverse sexual size dimorphism in the hummingbird family, although in this case the male is the larger sex. This divergence in size likely influences foraging strategies, with males able to dominate high-quality floral resources in their montane cloud forest habitat, while females may exploit a broader range of less contested feeding sites, a pattern observed in several other large-bodied trochilids.

Reproductive output in Eugenes fulgens is constrained by the species' life-history pace and the challenging environment of its highland pine-oak forests. Females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], and within that single reproductive event, they lay exactly two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch]. This modest clutch size is characteristic of many hummingbirds and reflects the high per-offspring investment required to fledge a viable chick in a resource-limited environment. The first successful breeding event, or age at first reproduction, occurs approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] when the bird is maintained at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This interval means that most individuals defer their first clutch until the second breeding season following their own hatching, a period that allows them to complete their skeletal growth and accumulate the necessary body condition for the considerable energetic demands of egg formation and subsequent provisioning of the nestling.

Maximum lifespan and basal metabolic rate represent two key physiological axes that define this species' position along the slow-fast continuum. The maximum recorded longevity for a Rivoli hummingbird in the wild, based on banding studies, is approximately 7.5 years [am = approximately 7.5 years], though this estimate is derived from a relatively small sample of recaptured individuals at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This lifespan is considered under a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Complementing this longevity, the resting metabolic rate of a post-absorptive adult at thermoneutrality has been measured at 18.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 18.5 milliliters per hour], recorded at an ambient temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This basal oxygen consumption is relatively high compared to similar-sized non-passerine birds, but is typical for hummingbirds, which support an energetically expensive hovering flight mode. The combination of a moderate lifespan for a bird of this body size and a high mass-specific metabolic rate places Eugenes fulgens firmly within the fast-living, high-energy strategy that characterises the Trochilidae as a whole.
